title: Beware "Yes", Master "No"
coreMove: Invite a protected no so the other side can become honest without feeling cornered.
sourcePressure: The source says yes can be a trap, while no-oriented questions preserve control, increase safety, and draw out deeper honesty after labeling has reduced friction.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer must not romanticize refusal or claim every no is useful apart from context and safety.

hook: A child says no and feels empowered
tryThisNow: Ask a question that gets no

exampleSpecs.domain: public defender plea discussion with a skeptical client
exampleSpecs.audience: a defender who needs truthful risk tolerance rather than a pressured agreement
exampleSpecs.stakes: the client may accept a plea he does not understand and later withdraw trust
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the defender asks 'Would it be a bad idea to slow down before you decide?' and the client finally says no, then explains the sentence length he fears
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a plea form lying beside a scratched interview-room phone

exampleSpecs.domain: architectural review for a historic storefront sign
exampleSpecs.audience: a shop owner facing a preservation board that keeps giving polite yeses and later objections
exampleSpecs.stakes: manufacturing the sign before real approval could waste the store's opening budget
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner stops asking if the design is acceptable and asks whether approving the brushed steel letters would be impossible, prompting the board chair to name the reflective finish issue
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a brushed steel letter sample wrapped in kraft paper on a hearing table

exampleSpecs.domain: nonprofit donor renewal after a failed campaign
exampleSpecs.audience: a development director trying to learn whether a major donor is truly out
exampleSpecs.stakes: the budget assumes a renewal that may be only a politeness yes
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director compares the old 'Can we count on you?' call with the no-oriented 'Would it be wrong to assume this year is off the table?' call that produces an honest condition
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a pledge card with the amount field left blank under a desk lamp

exampleSpecs.domain: shipyard repair estimate for an owner worried about overruns
exampleSpecs.audience: a yard manager who needs the owner to reveal the real budget ceiling
exampleSpecs.stakes: work may begin under false approval and stall when hidden cash limits appear
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager asks whether starting with the full refit would be reckless, giving the owner a safe no that opens a conversation about phased repairs
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a barnacle-scraped propeller resting on a wooden cradle near the lift bay

exampleSpecs.domain: software security exception request at a bank
exampleSpecs.audience: a product lead who keeps hearing yes from risk reviewers and then getting blocked
exampleSpecs.stakes: a release date will slip unless reviewers can safely say what they cannot accept
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the lead replaces 'Are we approved?' with 'Would it be unsafe to ship this exception?' and the reviewer finally says no to the current logging gap
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a risk waiver tab open beside a failed audit screenshot

exampleSpecs.audience: a market manager mediating between two vendors who keep agreeing in public and complaining later
exampleSpecs.stakes: the Saturday map may collapse if the hidden refusal stays private
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager asks each vendor whether the proposed aisle swap would be unacceptable, and one finally names the cold-storage distance as the true issue
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a laminated stall map pinned under a crate of peaches before sunrise

skillTargets: rewrite a yes-seeking question as a no-oriented safety question
identify a false yes in a scenario
analyze why protected refusal produces better information
evaluate when chasing no would become performative or hostile

tryThisNowSpec: Take one request where you usually ask for yes and rewrite it as a no-oriented question that lets the other person reject the unsafe path without embarrassment.
sourceAnchorsNote: source contains no named anecdote for this chapter

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: prevents the timestamp+named-protagonist template from dominating the chapter

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm — a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following 'concrete anchor -> abstract rule -> elaboration'
